The nominal speed of shellac discs from the early 1900s to the 1950s; a 12-inch side held about four and a half minutes.
The number etched in a disc’s run-out groove that identifies the recording; a take number says which attempt was issued.
Copying a disc or tape into a digital file; the stylus, playback speed, equalisation and noise reduction chosen all shape what you hear.
Free of copyright. A composition and a recording of it have separate terms, so out-of-copyright music can sit on a protected recording.
The Hall’s graph of relative level within one recording: where it grows stronger or quieter, never loudness or a comparison between recordings.
Matching a score’s bars to times in a recording by software; the Hall marks such timings provisional until a listener has checked them by ear.
Using a recognisable passage of another work, or a chant or tune, inside a new piece, openly or as an allusion.
Two senses: in Renaissance and Baroque practice, reworking existing music into a new piece; today, imitation that mocks.
Taking another work’s plan — its form, its bass, its procedure — as the pattern for a new piece, without quoting its notes.
A piece made in honour of another composer or person, often in their style or forms; a tombeau is an homage in memory of the dead.
Rewriting a piece for different instruments, from keyboard to orchestra or the reverse; a transcription stays close to the original’s notes.
How firmly a connection or fact is supported: documented (a source states it), inferred (the evidence points to it) or disputed (sources disagree).
The dominant chord followed by the tonic, both in root position: the strongest full stop in tonal harmony.
A phrase that ends on the dominant chord, which sounds unfinished and asks for a continuation.
A dominant chord that resolves to a chord other than the tonic, usually the minor chord on the sixth degree (V–vi), so the expected close is denied.
The subdominant chord moving to the tonic (IV–I), the “Amen” cadence: gentler and less final than dominant to tonic.
